extracted.intended_audience: life sciences companies and patent practitioners (in-house counsel, biotech/pharma patent attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on prosecuting, drafting, and defending composition-of-matter patents in chemical and life sciences, including eligibility under §101, §112 written description/enablement, Markush drafting, Hatch-Waxman ANDA litigation, and PTAB IPR defenses. Emphasizes claim drafting choices to maximize portfolio protection and litigation-readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 Patent-Eligible Subject Matter for Chemical Compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 101, a composition of matter patent covers any novel combination of chemical elements or compounds with a definite structural identity, and the composition must be non-naturally occurring or modified to confer markedly different characteristics from its natural form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed composition is 'made by man' (Diamond v. Chakrabarty) and not a product of nature (Mayo v. Prometheus; Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics). Natural laws and naturally occurring substances are ineligible; laboratory-created modifications (e.g., cDNA) may be eligible. Practitioners should perform a fact-intensive analysis of structural distinctiveness to assess § 101 risk during prosecution and post-grant challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myriad cDNA Distinction and Biological Composition Claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriad established that naturally occurring DNA sequences are products of nature ineligible under § 101 while preserving eligibility for complementary DNA (cDNA) because it is a laboratory-created molecule lacking non-coding intron sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For gene therapies and nucleic acid therapeutics, structure claims should focus on engineered molecules (e.g., cDNA or otherwise modified sequences) rather than naturally occurring sequences. Biotech patent counsel should evaluate whether a proposed biological composition achieves the structural distinctiveness required to survive USPTO examination and post-grant validity challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement (§112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must demonstrate the inventor possessed the full scope of the claimed invention at filing; disclosure of representative species and structural features common to the genus is required as an independent obligation from enablement (Ariad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting genus or broad composition claims, ensure the specification includes representative examples and identifies structural features shared across the claimed members. Broad claims that extend beyond supported examples risk invalidation for lack of written description. Counsel should align claim breadth to the specification's exemplified embodiments from the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement (§112) for Broad Genus Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement requires that the specification teach how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; failure to enable the full claimed scope can invalidate broad biological and pharmaceutical composition claims (e.g., Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether practicing the full breadth of claims would require substantial additional experimentation. If so, narrow claims or add exemplar embodiments and technical guidance to satisfy enablement. Work with prosecution specialists to match claim scope to the disclosure and experimental support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush Group Drafting Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Markush claim drafting allows a closed-list phrasing (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of') to define a class of chemical substituents so a single claim can cover multiple structural variants of a chemical compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members of a Markush group must share a single structural feature essential to the activity of all compounds in the group. Draft Markush groups with structural coherence and ensure the specification provides adequate support (representative species) for the listed members; overly broad Markush groups that include variants not exemplified may face written description and enablement challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing Markush Breadth with Specification Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must balance the breadth of the defined Markush group against supporting examples because extending to variants not exemplified may trigger Written Description challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit Markush lists to structurally coherent choices and provide representative examples across the chemical space. Consider dependent claims and exemplar embodiments to shore up support for broader independent Markush claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents and Prosecution History Estoppel in Markush Context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Doctrine of Equivalents interacts with Markush boundaries because prosecution history estoppel may bar equivalents for variants deliberately excluded from the closed list during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful during claim amendments and argument that narrowing a Markush list can create estoppel that limits later equivalence arguments. Preserve arguments and record where possible to avoid unintended estoppel consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatch-Waxman ANDA Litigation Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In ANDA litigation, a generic manufacturer will often challenge pharmaceutical composition patents under §§ 101, 102, 103, and 112 while contesting claim scope via Markman proceedings; bioequivalence data from FDA approval can be used to argue the generic product falls within the literal scope or that a claim is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holders should prepare for simultaneous multi-issue invalidity attacks and claim construction disputes. Retain counsel experienced in both chemistry and pharmaceutical litigation and coordinate patent strategy with regulatory and bioequivalence evidence considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Search and Chemical Space Mapping for Claim Drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: A robust prosecution strategy begins with a prior art search mapping the relevant chemical space to determine the minimum structural differentiation required for novelty and non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comprehensive prior art and chemical space analysis to set the baseline for how broadly to claim structures. Identify distinguishing structural features that confer patentability and craft claims around those minimum differentiators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Drafting Practices for Portfolio Protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims should be drafted at the broadest structurally supportable scope using Markush formats while dependent claims should anchor preferred embodiments with the strongest experimental support; continuation applications can build a layered claim portfolio as data develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft broad independent claims that are adequately supported and follow with narrower dependent claims backed by experimental data to preserve fallback positions. Use continuations strategically to pursue multiple claim scopes as development and data evolve. Consider patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. § 156 to compensate for regulatory delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB IPR Defense Strategies for Composition Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: When challenged via inter partes review before the PTAB, effective defenses include filing a preliminary response challenging the petitioner's claim construction before institution, and submitting expert declarations contextualizing the composition's structural novelty within the relevant scientific field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare expert evidence early, challenge claim constructions at the institution stage, and consider claim amendments under 37 C.F.R. § 42.121 to add structural limitations that distinguish asserted prior art. Evaluate licensing or settlement options to preserve commercial exclusivity when claims narrow during PTAB proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Claim Amendments under 37 C.F.R. § 42.121
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim amendments during PTAB proceedings can add structural limitations distinguishing the composition from asserted prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether proposed amendments will preserve patentable scope and commercial value; amendments can avoid institution or defeat grounds but may narrow enforceable rights. Coordinate technical expert input to craft defensible amendment language that maps to the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated Lifecycle Strategy (Prosecution, Freedom-to-Operate, PTAB Readiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic prosecution and enforcement requires coordinating claim drafting, prosecution history management, freedom-to-operate analysis, and PTAB litigation readiness into a unified lifecycle strategy to protect long-term exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate litigation risks during initial drafting—failures to foresee challenges can permanently narrow commercially valuable scope. Integrate freedom-to-operate analyses, prosecution choices, and PTAB/ANDA defense planning when building and maintaining a composition-of-matter portfolio.
